t: Minimum XOR Sum of Two Arrays — Assignment by Bitmask
o: We must permute nums2 so the elementwise XOR sum with nums1 is minimal: the cost is the sum over i of nums1[i] XOR permuted[i]. Example 1: nums1 = [1,2], nums2 = [2,3] — pairing 1 with 3 gives 1 XOR 3 = 2 and 2 with 2 gives 0, so the answer is 2; the greedy-looking pairing (1 with 2) would already spend 3. Example 2: nums1 = [1,0,3] against [5,3,4] resolves to the rearrangement [5,4,3], costing (1 XOR 5) + (0 XOR 4) + (3 XOR 3) = 4 + 4 + 0 = 8. No greedy rule survives because XOR cost is not monotone in either operand alone — a cheap early match can strand an expensive leftover. The decisive constraint is n <= 14: at most 2^14 subsets of nums2 exist, so we can afford to remember, for every subset already consumed, the cheapest way to have consumed it. That is exactly a bitmask dynamic program over assignment decisions.
k: n <= 14 makes every subset of nums2 an addressable DP state (at most 2^14 masks).
If mask marks the nums2 elements already paired, they necessarily belong to the first popcount(mask) elements of nums1, collapsing one index dimension.
XOR costs admit no greedy exchange argument, so locally cheapest pairings can be globally suboptimal.

a.i: Recursively build the bijection: at position i try every unused nums2[j], add nums1[i] XOR nums2[j] to the running total and recurse. Branch-and-bound pruning (cut when the partial total reaches the best complete sum) keeps constants small but cannot beat factorial growth — this baseline exists to motivate memoization.
s: Recursively assign an unused nums2[j] to nums1[i] and accumulate nums1[i] XOR nums2[j].
Prune any branch whose running total is no longer below the best complete sum found.
Record the total whenever i reaches n.
a.t: O(n * n!) — all permutations are visited in the worst case; pruning only improves constants.
a.sp: O(n) — recursion depth plus the used flags.

a.i: Define dfs(i, mask) as the minimum cost of matching nums1[i..n-1] against whichever nums2 entries mask leaves free. Trying each free j gives dfs(i, mask) = min over j of (nums1[i] XOR nums2[j]) + dfs(i+1, mask | (1 << j)), with base case dfs(n, _) = 0. Only n * 2^n distinct states exist, so caching turns exponential branching into manageable work.
s: Memoize on (i, mask), where bit j of mask means nums2[j] is taken.
Transition: minimize the XOR cost plus the recursive result over every unset bit j.
a.t: O(n^2 * 2^n) — up to n transitions from each of n * 2^n states.
a.sp: O(n * 2^n) — the memo table indexed by position and mask.

a.i: Flip the direction: dp[mask] is the minimum cost when exactly the elements of mask are paired with the first popcount(mask) entries of nums1. The element matched last is nums1[popcount(mask) - 1], so dp[mask] = min over set bits low of dp[mask without low] + (nums1[i] XOR nums2[j]). Sweeping set bits with m &= m - 1 touches only live transitions and removes the i axis entirely, halving memory versus the memo table.
s: Set dp[0] = 0 and every other dp[mask] to infinity.
For each mask from 1 to 2^n - 1, let i = popcount(mask) - 1.
For each set bit low (corresponding element j), relax dp[mask] with dp[mask ^ low] + (nums1[i] XOR nums2[j]).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minimumXORSum(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums1)
        dp = [inf] * (1 << n)
        dp[0] = 0
        for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
            i = bin(mask).count('1') - 1
            m = mask
            while m:
                low = m & -m
                j = low.bit_length() - 1
                dp[mask] = min(dp[mask], dp[mask ^ low] + (nums1[i] ^ nums2[j]))
                m ^= low
        return dp[-1]

a.t: O(n * 2^n) — summed over all masks, each of the n * 2^(n-1) (mask, set-bit) pairs relaxes once.

w: Once n is around 20 or below, go straight to bitmask DP and mention permutation search only as motivation. Pitfalls: binding the nums1 index to popcount(mask) instead of carrying it as separate state, C++ operator precedence in (mask >> j) & 1, and noting values up to 10^7 keep every running total safely inside 32-bit integers. Follow-ups: maximizing instead of minimizing only flips the relaxation; for larger n, meet-in-the-middle halves the exponent.
